name: Hana Yilmaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, AI companies, unions or government. We do not sell or campaign for any side. Your answers are confidential. What is an ordinary day at work like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead the afternoon agents at a contact centre, take calls when a refund has been disputed twice, and write a handover sheet for the evening team. I have a two-year college diploma, but the part I use most is keeping a promise straight across three shifts. I like putting a customer's problem right; I don't like a new screen appearing without anyone explaining who is responsible for errors.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the usual call system has had a fancy name put on it, and I'd carry on answering customers. If the new button saves a minute, fine, but someone still has to own the complaint.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't use AI now, and I wouldn't rush to learn it for a tiny saving. I'm on ordinary pay for a lead, with four months of expenses put away, so I don't see this picture taking my job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the shift handover sheet and check disputed refunds the way I do now. In the first year of this plateau, I'd ask my manager for a clear instruction if the new button becomes compulsory, then keep my four-month reserve intact.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Quite settled. The busiest Friday calls still wear me out, but they were there before this talk of AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What is on your handover sheet?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I write who called back, what was promised, and which refund is still waiting for approval. Otherwise the evening team has to guess, and a customer has to tell the story from the start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why insist on an instruction for one button?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If a tool changes a refund, I want to know who checks it and who fixes a mistake. I don't want an agent blamed later for clicking something we were told to click without a rule.

S0.quote: I don't want an agent blamed later for clicking something we were told to click without a rule.
say: I would say the **new button** changes little about answering customers.
I would insist someone still owns each **complaint**.
think: I do not use AI and see no reason to rush for a **small saving**.
I have **four months** saved and expect my lead shifts to continue.
do: Keep the **handover sheet** and check disputed refunds as usual.
Ask my manager for **written instructions** if the new button becomes compulsory.
Keep my **four-month reserve** for ordinary emergencies.
feel: **Settled**, despite the usual tiring Friday queue.
fieldNote: Hana’s concern is **accountability** for refund errors, not excitement or fear over a minor tool.
Her **four-month cushion** and stable lead role make the plateau feel manageable.

steps.text: Keep recording callbacks and disputed refunds on the handover sheet
Ask for written instructions if the AI button becomes compulsory

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the team not to call a faster queue a better service until we count the complaints that come back. I'd ask for the new targets in writing before I train anyone on them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I know calls and chats are exactly the kind of work this system can take. I'm good at the difficult calls, but a manager could leave one lead with twice the queue and fewer agents; four months saved would go quickly if my hours were cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep a paper tally of repeat calls and ask my manager to compare it with the speed report. If the new system reaches our centre, I'd sit through the required training before using it on live refunds; in its first year, if my hours shrink, I'd apply to the other centres in town rather than resign first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uncomfortable. The work I know could change under my hands, and I don't enjoy practising on customers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with the repeat-call tally?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take a week's figures to the manager and ask whether the queue really got shorter or just made people call again. If the numbers look bad, I'd ask for a slower rollout.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You would train on a tool you dislike?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the centre requires it, yes. I want supervised practice and a way to undo AI refund mistakes. I'm not going to pretend I already know the tool because someone played a video in the break room.

S1.quote: I want supervised practice and a way to undo AI refund mistakes.
say: I would ask for **repeat-call counts** before calling a faster queue better service.
I would request **written targets** before training other agents.
think: I know my **calls and chats** are exposed, even though I handle the difficult ones well.
I fear a smaller team could cut my **hours** and drain four months of savings.
do: Count **repeat calls** and compare them with the speed report.
Attend **supervised training** if the centre makes AI use compulsory.
Apply to **other centres** if my hours shrink, keeping this job until I have an offer.
feel: **Uncomfortable** with changes to familiar work and live customer cases.
fieldNote: Hana wants a **paper tally** before accepting a speed claim from management.
She will learn a tool only with **supervision** and a way to correct mistakes.

steps.text: Count repeat calls for a week before accepting new speed targets
Attend supervised AI training if the centre requires live use
Apply to other local contact centres if her hours shrink

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the centre owes us straight dates and proper notice if the call work is going. I would ask them to tell customers where a real person can hear an appeal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2028 a cheaper system could take nearly every call I handle. Robots coming around 2031 don't delay that for a headset. I have four months saved, but I might have to use it just to keep the rent paid while I look for work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask my manager this week for a written staffing timetable and stop the holiday savings transfer. In the first year after AGI arrives, if the centre ends my role, I'd apply to the local hospital's reception desk if it still hires people, and I'd claim any help I qualify for before using all my reserve.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm frightened enough to lie awake. I can fill out applications, but I cannot make a desk vacancy appear when every office is changing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why hospital reception?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mother had appointments there last year, and the receptionist helped us find the right ward when the signs were confusing. I could do that sort of patient-facing work, but I'd check whether the post still includes people rather than just screen forms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your partner that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my partner Sam that I have four months of bills saved and we should plan the rent together. I'd cancel the holiday before asking Sam to cover a shortfall; Sam has a job, but our rent is a shared bill.

S2.quote: I can fill out applications, but I cannot make a desk vacancy appear when every office is changing.
say: I would demand **straight dates** and proper notice if call roles are going.
I would ask for a **human appeal** route for customers.
think: I expect AGI could take nearly all my **calls** by 2028.
I know the **2031 robot date** does not protect headset work, and four months saved may disappear during a search.
do: Ask my manager for **staffing dates** now and about support if my role ends.
Stop the **holiday transfer** and cancel the trip if income falls.
Apply for **hospital reception** only if it still has a people-facing vacancy after a role cut.
feel: **Frightened**, awake over rent and scarce vacancies.
fieldNote: Hana sees **hospital reception** through her mother’s visit, while recognising that desk work may also change.
She treats her **four-month reserve** as rent protection, not free money for a speculative course.

steps.text: Ask the manager for a written staffing timetable
Stop holiday savings and cancel the trip if income falls
Apply for a people-facing hospital reception vacancy after a role cut
Claim any support I qualify for before spending the full rent reserve

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell colleagues five years is enough time for a proper plan, but only if the centre puts dates and training places on paper. I'd still want a person to hear appeals when the software gives a customer the wrong answer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could stay long enough to save more and learn what other employers actually want. AGI by 2031 still reaches our calls first; the robots in 2034 are not the part that worries me most.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the hospital about reception vacancies and required certificates this year, without leaving my lead job. If there is a paid course with a real opening at the end, I'd enrol next year; in the first year after AGI arrives, if my hours vanish, I'd apply for that hospital opening or another staffed desk role after checking the pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still worried, but I can use five years to look before I jump. I would rather be a little slow than spend our rent reserve on the wrong course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What makes a course real enough?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I want the course name, fee, time off, and a hospital person who can say whether it counts for hiring. A poster promising new skills without an actual vacancy doesn't answer that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you try the centre’s AI training as well?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would take required training if they let me practise with someone watching. I would not volunteer to run the whole team's training when I still need to learn it myself.

S3.quote: I would rather be a little slow than spend our rent reserve on the wrong course.
say: I would ask for **dates and training places** on paper before calling five years a plan.
I would keep a **human appeal** route for wrong customer answers.
think: I could build savings and check **real vacancies** before 2031.
I know **thinking AI** reaches calls first; 2034 robots are a later concern.
do: Ask the **hospital** this year about reception jobs and required certificates.
Enrol in a **paid course** next year only if it leads to a real opening.
Apply for a **staffed desk job** if my call hours vanish, after checking pay.
feel: **Worried**, with time to check before spending the rent reserve.
fieldNote: Hana measures a course by fees, time off, and a **hiring contact**.
Extra time lets her keep the **lead job** while testing whether hospital reception still needs people.

steps.text: Ask the hospital which staffed reception jobs and certificates are available
Enrol in paid reception training if a real opening follows
Apply for a staffed desk vacancy if call hours vanish

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we should use the decade to keep the service decent and let staff plan around real dates. I'd ask the centre to give agents a written route to other jobs, not just a pile of training links.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years would put me at 37, with time to save and see which desk jobs still exist. I could learn a new system if I had to, but I wouldn't build my whole future on a tool I haven't seen work. Robots around 2039 do not change the fact that calls change in 2036.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the lead job and increase the monthly emergency transfer while my pay holds. Over the decade I'd visit the hospital jobs desk once a year and take a paid course only if a clear opening requires it; in the first year after AGI arrives, I'd stay if the centre still offers full hours, otherwise apply for a staffed reception post with confirmed pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel less cornered. Ten years gives me time to check the facts instead of guessing from a headline.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ever use AI on calls yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If it became the standard tool and someone taught me properly, yes. I would check each refund against the account record and ask who signs off when the tool is wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you leave before 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A firm offer with dependable hours and pay would do it. I wouldn't leave for a hopeful interview just because a future date is on a card.

S4.quote: I wouldn't leave for a hopeful interview just because a future date is on a card.
say: I would request **real dates** and a written route to other jobs.
I would ask the centre to keep **service quality** in view while changing tools.
think: At 37 in 2036, I would have time to save and inspect **desk vacancies**.
I know **calls change first**, while 2039 robots are a later issue.
do: Keep my **lead job** and increase emergency savings while full pay holds.
Visit the **hospital jobs desk** yearly to check staffed reception roles.
Take a **paid course** only if a confirmed opening requires it.
feel: **Less cornered**, because I can check facts over a decade.
fieldNote: Hana would adopt compulsory AI with **proper instruction** and clear responsibility for refund errors.
She would leave early only for a **firm offer** with dependable pay and hours.

steps.text: Keep leading customer calls while full shifts remain
Increase the monthly emergency account transfer while pay holds
Check staffed hospital reception vacancies once each year
Take paid reception training if a confirmed opening requires it

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most. The calls might go before I can see what other employers still need, and four months saved isn't a new salary. Written notice, clear vacancies with pay, and supervised training attached to real work would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who signs the refund correction when a customer appeals. Every system has an error now and then, and a customer should be able to find the person who can fix it.

headlineQuote: The calls might go before I can see what other employers still need, and four months saved isn't a new salary.
portrait: Hana is a **27-year-old lead** at a contact centre, valued for disputed refunds and careful handovers across shifts.
She has a **two-year diploma**, typical pay, four months saved, a partner sharing rent, and some similar jobs nearby.
She never uses AI now and asks for **written rules**, supervised practice, and evidence before changing familiar work.
Fast **2028 AGI** alarms her; longer timelines give her room to check staffed hospital jobs and protect her rent reserve.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could end her call role before she knows which staffed jobs still exist.
whatWouldHelp: **Written notice**, verified vacancies with pay, and supervised training tied to real work would help her change safely.
